alignment.note: Greek uses a single imperfect ἔλεγεν ('he was saying'); the Peshitta renders the durative aspect periphrastically with ܐܡܪ ܗܘܐ (perfect + enclitic ܗܘܐ), a standard Syriac construction for the imperfect/customary past. The Vulgate dicebat captures the same imperfective force in one word.

The Vulgate separates the dative illis from the following oratio recta with an editorial colon (token 3); Greek marks the same boundary with a raised dot (·) attached to αὐτοῖς·, while Syriac leaves the juncture unpunctuated.

Greek λέγω encodes the first-person subject inflectionally; the Peshitta makes it explicit with the independent pronoun ܐܢܐ ('I') after ܐܡܪ, a normal Syriac analytic construction. The Latin dico parallels the Greek synthetic form without an overt pronoun.

Greek ὅτι and Latin quia introduce the content clause as a conjunction; the Syriac fuses the complementiser with the existential particle as ܕܐܝܬ (relative/complementiser d- + ܐܝܬ 'there is'), so the boundary between 'that' and 'there are' is morphologically merged.
Existential predicate εἰσίν / ܐܝܬ (within ܕܐܝܬ) / sunt; the Syriac form is shared with the preceding complementiser token.

Greek indefinite τινες ('some [persons]') and Latin quidam are pronominal; the Syriac makes the referent concrete with the noun ܐܢܫܐ ('people, men'), an idiomatic specification of the indefinite plural.

Greek uses an articular perfect participle τῶν ἑστηκότων ('of those standing'); the Vulgate mirrors this with a substantival present participle (de hic stantibus), whereas the Peshitta employs a relative clause ܕܩܝܡܝܢ ('who are standing') — a construction-level rather than lexical difference.

Greek and Latin attest an explicit relative pronoun (οἵτινες / qui) heading the following clause; the Peshitta has no separate relative token here, since the relativising d- is prefixed to the negated verb in the next group (ܕܠܐ).

Greek employs the emphatic double negation οὐ μή with the aorist subjunctive to express strong future denial ('shall by no means'); the Latin renders it with simple non + future gustabunt, and the Syriac with the relativised negative ܕܠܐ — all conveying emphatic prohibition but with differing negation strategies.

Greek combines the temporal conjunction ἕως with the modal particle ἂν before the subjunctive, marking contingency; both the Syriac ܥܕܡܐ and the Latin donec render the temporal force with a single particle and no separate modal marker.

Greek expresses 'the kingdom' with article + noun (τὴν βασιλείαν) and a following genitive τοῦ θεοῦ; the Syriac compresses the construct into a single suffixed form ܡܠܟܘܬܗ ('his kingdom', with the genitive realised by the pronominal suffix anticipating ܕܐܠܗܐ), a typical Semitic anticipatory-suffix construction.
Genitive of God τοῦ θεοῦ / ܕܐܠܗܐ / Dei.

Greek uses the perfect participle ἐληλυθυῖαν ('having come', stressing completed arrival); the Vulgate present participle veniens reads as 'coming', a slight aspectual shift, while the Syriac finite relative ܕܐܬܬ ('which has come') aligns with the Greek perfective sense.
Prepositional phrase ἐν δυνάμει / ܒܚܝܠܐ / in virtute, 'with/in power'.
